title: Terraform Providers & Resources: The Handbook
summary: A dense field guide to how Terraform providers plug into the core, how resource schemas define arguments and attributes, what every meta-argument really does, and how version constraints and lock files keep plans reproducible.

chapters.title: Providers: What They Actually Are
points: A provider is a separate binary plugin; terraform core talks to it over gRPC on localhost, not in-process
Core owns the graph, state, and plan/apply lifecycle; the provider owns API calls and schema
Providers are downloaded by `terraform init` into `.terraform/providers/<registry>/<namespace>/<name>/<version>/<os_arch>/`
Source address anatomy: `registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws` — hostname / namespace / type; short form `hashicorp/aws`
`required_providers` inside the `terraform {}` block is the only correct place to declare source + version
A bare `provider "aws" {}` block configures, it does not declare — relying on implicit declaration guesses namespace `hashicorp`
Provider types: managed resource providers (aws, google), utility providers (random, null, time, local), logical providers (tls, http)
The provider protocol version (5 vs 6) must match what your Terraform CLI speaks; protocol 6 needs Terraform >= 1.0
Provider configuration is evaluated at apply time, so it cannot depend on values unknown until apply
Example: `terraform { required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 5.0" } } }`
`terraform providers` prints the provider dependency tree including inherited module requirements
Provider plugin cache (`plugin_cache_dir` in CLI config) avoids re-downloading the same binary per workspace
Third-party and in-house providers live under a different namespace or a private registry; source address changes, syntax does not
Gotcha: deleting `.terraform/` is safe and recoverable; deleting `.terraform.lock.hcl` silently allows version drift

chapters.title: Resource Schema: The Contract
points: Every resource type ships a schema: a map of attribute names to types, plus behavior flags
Behavior flags: Required, Optional, Computed, ForceNew, Sensitive, Deprecated
Required = you must set it. Optional = you may. Computed = provider fills it in
Optional+Computed is the tricky combo: you may set it, and if you do not, the API supplies a default that Terraform records
Types: string, number, bool, list(T), set(T), map(T), object({...}), plus nested blocks
Set vs list: sets are unordered and deduplicated, so reordering causes no diff; lists are index-sensitive and reordering does
Nested blocks come in modes: single, list, set — this decides whether you write one block or repeat it
`terraform providers schema -json` dumps the full machine-readable schema for any provider you have installed
Schema is versioned per resource; state upgraders migrate old state shapes forward on read
A resource address is `type.name` (e.g. `aws_instance.web`); the type's prefix binds it to a provider by convention
Provider-defined validation runs at plan time (`ValidateFunc` / framework validators) and fails before any API call
Data sources have their own schema, almost entirely Computed with a few Required lookup arguments
Example: `aws_s3_bucket.bucket` is Optional+Computed — omit it and AWS generates a name Terraform then stores
Gotcha: registry docs are generated from the schema, so if docs and schema disagree, the schema wins

chapters.title: Arguments vs Attributes
points: Argument = input you write in the config block. Attribute = value you read back with `resource.name.field`
Every argument is readable as an attribute; not every attribute is settable as an argument
Read-only attributes are the Computed-only ones: `id`, `arn`, `private_ip`, `endpoint`, timestamps
Setting a read-only attribute is a config error: `Can't configure a value for "arn": its value will be decided automatically`
The universal attribute is `id` — every managed resource has one, it is a string, and it is the provider's remote identifier
Referencing an attribute creates an implicit dependency edge in the graph — this is the primary ordering mechanism
Unknown values: at plan time a not-yet-created attribute renders as `(known after apply)`
Unknown values propagate — one unknown attribute makes every expression that consumes it unknown
Unknowns cannot be used in `count`, `for_each` keys, or provider config; that is what causes most "value depends on resource attributes" errors
Data source attributes are read during plan (or refresh) and are known early, unless the data source depends on an unknown
Comparison row: argument -> written by you -> validated at plan; attribute -> written by API -> resolved at apply
Sensitive attributes propagate their sensitivity through expressions and get redacted in plan output
Example: `subnet_id = aws_subnet.a.id` reads an attribute and orders subnet before instance in one stroke
Gotcha: `depends_on` is only needed when the dependency is real but invisible to the expression graph (IAM policy before instance profile use)

chapters.title: Meta-Arguments I: count & for_each
points: Meta-arguments are core features, not provider features — they work on every resource type identically
`count = n` creates n instances addressed `type.name[0]` ... `[n-1]`, with `count.index` available inside
`for_each` takes a map or a set of strings and creates instances addressed `type.name["key"]`, with `each.key` and `each.value`
count and for_each are mutually exclusive on one block
The killer difference: count keys by position, so removing the middle element shifts and recreates every element after it
for_each keys by identity, so removing one element destroys exactly one instance
Rule of thumb: count for identical or on/off resources, for_each for a keyed collection of distinct things
`count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0` is the standard conditional-resource idiom
for_each keys must be known at plan time — computed values in keys give "The for_each map cannot be determined until apply"
Convert a list to a valid for_each set with `toset(var.names)`; convert objects with `{ for o in var.objs : o.name => o }`
With count/for_each the whole resource becomes a list/map: `aws_instance.web[*].id` (splat) or `values(aws_instance.web)[*].id`
Migrating count to for_each without `moved` blocks destroys and recreates everything
`moved { from = aws_instance.web[0]  to = aws_instance.web["a"] }` performs the rename in state, no API calls
Gotcha: `for_each` over a set gives `each.key == each.value`; over a map, `each.value` is the map's value

chapters.title: Meta-Arguments II: provider, depends_on, lifecycle
points: `provider = aws.west` selects a non-default provider instance for that resource
`depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy.p]` forces ordering when no attribute reference exists
depends_on takes references only, never strings, and makes the dependent's plan more conservative (more unknowns)
`lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }` builds the replacement first; needed for resources behind a load balancer or with unique-name constraints
create_before_destroy propagates to dependencies — if a dependency cannot be created first, the whole chain must adopt it
`prevent_destroy = true` turns any destroy plan into a hard error; it is a guardrail, not a lock (removing the block removes the guard)
`ignore_changes = [tags, ami]` tells Terraform to stop diffing those attributes after creation
`ignore_changes = all` freezes the whole resource; useful for adopting drifted infrastructure
`replace_triggered_by = [aws_instance.web.id]` forces replacement when another resource changes
`lifecycle { precondition { ... } }` and `postcondition` assert invariants at plan and apply time
Lifecycle blocks accept only literal expressions — no variables, because they are evaluated before the graph walk
`-replace=aws_instance.web` on the CLI is the modern taint; `terraform taint` is deprecated
Comparison: prevent_destroy blocks apply; ignore_changes hides diffs; replace_triggered_by forces churn
Gotcha: ignore_changes on an argument does not stop the initial create from using it — it only silences later drift

chapters.title: Provider Configuration & Aliases
points: One `provider` block per provider is the default instance; every resource of that type uses it implicitly
`alias = "west"` creates a second, named instance of the same provider with different settings
Aliased instances are selected explicitly: `provider = aws.west` on the resource, or `providers = { aws = aws.west }` on a module
Common alias uses: multi-region, multi-account (assume_role), multi-cluster kubernetes
Credentials should come from the environment (`AWS_PROFILE`, `GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS`) not hardcoded arguments
Child modules should NOT declare their own provider blocks — they inherit or receive them
A module with its own provider block cannot be removed cleanly and cannot use `for_each`/`count` on the module
Declare what a module needs with `required_providers` + `configuration_aliases = [aws.replica]`
Default (unaliased) providers are inherited automatically by child modules; aliased ones must be passed explicitly
Provider config values can reference variables and locals but not resource attributes computed at apply
Example: `provider "aws" { alias = "west"  region = "us-west-2" }` then `resource "aws_s3_bucket" "b" { provider = aws.west }`
`terraform init` errors with "Missing required provider" when a module's configuration_aliases is not satisfied by the caller
Provider-level `default_tags` (AWS) and `ignore_tags` apply across every resource that instance manages
Gotcha: destroying resources whose provider alias was deleted leaves state you cannot plan — remove the resources first, then the alias

chapters.title: Version Constraints & the Lock File
points: Constraint operators: `=`, `!=`, `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`, `~>`, and comma-joined conjunctions
`~> 5.0` means >= 5.0 and < 6.0 (pessimistic at the minor level, one segment shorter than written)
`~> 5.31.0` means >= 5.31.0 and < 5.32.0 (pessimistic at the patch level)
`>= 5.0, < 6.0` is the explicit long form of `~> 5.0`
Providers follow semver: major = breaking schema changes, minor = new resources/arguments, patch = fixes
`.terraform.lock.hcl` records the exact selected version plus provider binary hashes (`h1:` and `zh:`)
COMMIT the lock file. It is the reproducibility guarantee, the analogue of package-lock.json
`terraform init -upgrade` re-resolves within the constraints and rewrites the lock file
`terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64` adds hashes for other platforms so CI does not fail
"Provider produced inconsistent... checksums" on CI usually means the lock has only your local platform's hashes
`required_version = ">= 1.5"` in the terraform block constrains the CLI itself, separately from providers
Constraints from root and every module are intersected; an empty intersection is an init failure
Strategy: loose-ish constraints (`~> 5.0`) in reusable modules, tight in root configs, exactness from the lock file
Gotcha: pinning `= 5.31.0` in a shared module is antisocial — it makes the module uncomposable with any sibling that needs another patch

chapters.title: Resource Lifecycle: Plan, Diff, Apply
points: Order per run: init -> refresh (read real state) -> plan (diff desired vs real) -> apply (call APIs) -> write state
Plan symbols: `+` create, `-` destroy, `~` update in place, `-/+` destroy then create, `+/-` create then destroy (CBD), `<=` read data source
Replacement happens when a changed argument is ForceNew in the schema; the plan prints `# forces replacement`
Update-in-place happens when the provider can express the change as an API update call
Refresh detects drift — changes made outside Terraform show up as a diff back toward config
`-refresh-only` plans show drift without proposing to fix it; useful for auditing
`terraform plan -out=tfplan` then `terraform apply tfplan` guarantees you apply exactly what you reviewed
`-target=aws_instance.web` narrows the graph; it is a break-glass tool, not a workflow
Terraform applies in dependency order and parallelizes independent nodes (default `-parallelism=10`)
Destroy walks the graph in reverse dependency order
"Provider produced inconsistent result after apply" is a provider bug: the returned state did not match the plan
`terraform import` (or an `import {}` block) binds existing infrastructure to a resource address without creating it
`import { to = aws_s3_bucket.b  id = "my-bucket" }` is the config-driven, plannable form added in 1.5
Gotcha: `terraform state rm` orphans real infrastructure — it forgets, it does not delete

chapters.title: Trade-offs, Cost, and Common Mistakes
points: Provider API calls dominate wall-clock time; refresh is O(resources) network round trips
Big flat root modules refresh everything on every plan — split state to keep plans fast
Mistake: no version constraint at all — a provider major bump silently breaks the next init on a fresh machine
Mistake: lock file in .gitignore — every machine and CI runner resolves a different version
Mistake: hardcoded credentials in provider blocks — they land in the repo and often in state
State stores attribute values in plaintext, including passwords; sensitive markers only redact CLI output
Mistake: count over a list of names — inserting a name in the middle recreates the tail
Mistake: `ignore_changes = all` used as a bandage, hiding real drift forever
Mistake: provider blocks inside reusable modules — blocks module for_each and clean removal
Mistake: relying on `depends_on` where an attribute reference would express the same thing more precisely
Mistake: `-target` in normal operation, producing a state that never matches a full plan
Trade-off: many small states = fast plans, weak cross-cutting refactors; one big state = slow plans, easy references
Trade-off: `create_before_destroy` gives zero downtime but needs unique names and doubles capacity briefly
Trade-off: pinned exact versions give reproducibility, cost you security patches and drift the whole fleet at once

chapters.title: Summary: The Mental Model
points: Core = graph, state, plan. Provider = schema, API. gRPC between them. That single split explains most behavior
Schema is the source of truth: it decides Required/Optional/Computed and therefore argument vs attribute
Arguments go in, attributes come out, `id` always exists, referencing an attribute builds the dependency edge
`(known after apply)` means unknown; unknowns are contagious and forbidden in for_each keys, count, and provider config
Meta-arguments are core-level and universal: count, for_each, provider, depends_on, lifecycle
for_each keys by identity, count keys by position — that difference is the single biggest source of accidental destroys
Use `moved` blocks for any address change, `import` blocks for any adoption; both are plannable and reviewable
`~> 5.0` in config sets the range; `.terraform.lock.hcl` picks the point; commit the lock
Add multi-platform hashes with `terraform providers lock` before CI bites you
Aliases give you N configured instances of one provider; pass them into modules with `configuration_aliases`
ForceNew in schema = `-/+` in plan; pair with `create_before_destroy` when downtime is unacceptable
Read the plan symbols before every apply; save the plan file and apply exactly that
Checklist: source pinned, version constrained, lock committed, no credentials in HCL, no provider block in child modules
One line to keep: Terraform does not know your infrastructure — it knows the schema, the state, and what the provider told it last
